argument.notes: For each ordering, an interacting tuple has j1-j2 in {0,1,2}: its largest magnitude is at most three times its second largest. Each smaller shell has 2^(j+1) integers, so the two ell^1 bounds give at most 2*2^((j3+j4)/2) times the four shell norms. Nthird is at least 2^j3, including tied shell indices. Dropping j2>=j3 factors the nonnegative upper bound; shift Cauchy–Schwarz and the geometric sum bound both factors. Counting at most 24 orderings and three offsets, C=144/(1-2^(-1/2)) is one valid uniform choice. S003 bounds each finite positive partial sum by a containing finite-support truncation, establishing the full supremum and every subset restriction.

background_notes.fact: For nonnegative square-summable sequences u,v on Z (extended by zero where originally undefined) and integer s, sum_k u(k)v(s-k) <= ||u||_2||v||_2. For a finite set E, sum_{k in E}u(k) <= sqrt(|E|)*(sum_{k in E}u(k)^2)^(1/2). In particular these hold for the shell-restricted sequences used in S001.

grounds.reason: L1 gives nonnegativity and ell^2 membership, and the proof first works with finite support and shell restrictions.
The sequence norm is the counting-measure ell^2 norm on the specified integer domain.

background_notes.justification: Finite Cauchy–Schwarz follows by expanding the nonnegative sum of squares sum_k (t*u(k)-v(k))^2 and minimizing in t (with the zero-norm case immediate). Apply it to u(k),v(s-k); k -> s-k is a bijection of Z, so the reflected translate has the same squared norm. Applying it to u and the indicator of E gives the finite-set ell^1 bound. If an infinite sequence is involved, the same inequality for every finite partial sum gives the asserted nonnegative sum bound by its supremum.

background_notes.fact: For nonnegative U,V in ell^2(N_0), extended by zero at negative indices, and q>=0, sum_{J>=0} U(J)V(J-q) <= ||U||_2||V||_2. Also sum_{ell>=m>=0} h^(ell-m)U(ell)V(m) <= ||U||_2||V||_2/(1-h) for 0<h<1. The latter applies with h=2^(-1/2).

grounds.reason: Shell norm sequences are nonnegative and extended by zero at negative indices.
The paragraph specifies q in {0,1,2}, rewrites r=ell-m, and uses exactly the positive ratio h=2^(-1/2).
The finite-support setting ensures square-summable shell norm sequences; their squared norms are the disjoint shell sums of the input squares.

background_notes.justification: Cauchy–Schwarz bounds each shifted product sum by ||U||_2||V||_2, since a shift or a restriction of an index range cannot increase the squared norm here. For the second inequality first take a finite range and group by r=ell-m; the r-th contribution is at most h^r||U||_2||V||_2. The finite geometric identity gives sum_{r=0}^M h^r=(1-h^(M+1))/(1-h)<=1/(1-h). Taking suprema of finite nonnegative partial sums yields the bound. Since h^(M+1) tends to zero for 0<h<1, the infinite geometric sum equals 1/(1-h), as asserted in S002.

grounds.reason: S001 partitions all nonzero integers into exactly these disjoint shells under L1.
Xshell is defined to be the counting-measure ell^2 norm of each shell restriction.

background_notes.justification: The shells form a disjoint exhaustive partition of the nonzero integers. For finite support, grouping the finite sum of squared entries proves the identity directly, which is all S002 needs. In general the identity follows from the definition of a nonnegative sum as the supremum of finite subsums: every finite set of frequencies meets only finitely many shells, and finite subsums from finitely many shells can be combined. Restricting a sum of nonnegative squares gives the truncation inequality.
